front: Ask one friend in Italian how they are. Use stare.
notes: Here come asks how someone feels. English also reuses words. In “as a teacher”, as gives a role. In “as tall as me”, it compares.

front: Say “I work as a teacher” in Italian. Use lavorare and give your actual role.
notes: Come introduces the role you actually do. In this pattern the job title comes straight after come.

front: Say to a friend “You’re like a brother to me”.
answer: Sei come un fratello per me.
english: You’re like a brother to me.
pron: SEH-ee KOH-meh oon frah-TEHL-loh pehr MEH
notes: Come makes a comparison here. The phrase works even if you are unrelated.

front: Che lavoro fai? Which Italian word changes when you ask about Marta instead of tu? Give the word from the original question.
notes: Che lavoro fa Marta? Fai changes to fa. Lavoro stays the noun meaning job. The ending of fai already tells you the subject is tu.

front: In Che lavoro fai?, give the whole Italian phrase for the thing you do.
notes: You do what? What job. Che lavoro is the direct object, even at the start of the question.

front: Complete “I work in an office” with the first-person form of lavorare. ___ in un ufficio.
notes: Here lavoro is a verb. English does this too. In “I work here”, work is the verb. In “What work do you do?”, work is a noun.

front: Which two Italian verbs mean “I do” and “I work” in Faccio l’insegnante e lavoro in una scuola? Give them in sentence order.
notes: Each verb belongs to its own part of the sentence, joined by e (and). Both have the same understood subject, io.

front: You’re at the kitchen sink. Complete “I wash the dishes” with the verb lavare. ___ i piatti.
notes: Lavare → lavo (to wash → I wash). Lavorare → lavoro (to work → I work). The extra syllable changes the word.

front: In Lavo i piatti, say the Italian words that answer “I wash what?” Include the article.
notes: Think “I wash them”. The dishes are the direct object. The verb takes them directly, so this use is transitive.

front: In Lavoro in un ufficio, which whole Italian phrase answers “where?”
notes: In introduces a place. The sentence already works as Lavoro, “I work”. Here lavorare is intransitive.

front: In Lavoro il legno, say the Italian phrase for the material being shaped. Include the article.
notes: I work or shape the wood. Il legno is the direct object. Compare Lavoro in un ufficio, where the office is the place. The same verb has two uses.

front: Say “I work as a doctor” using fare and the masculine job title beginning with d.
notes: Use the definite article for fare + occupation. Other uses of fare allow different forms, as in faccio una torta or faccio sport.

front: Someone asks whether there is a doctor on the train. Say “I’m a doctor” with essere, the indefinite article and the masculine title beginning with d.
notes: Un introduces one member of a profession. The complete phrase un dottore identifies the speaker.

front: A patient asks which person is the doctor on duty. Say “I’m the doctor on duty” using essere and the masculine title beginning with d.
notes: Il picks out a particular doctor. Il dottore is singular. I dottori is plural.

front: Say “I’m a teacher” with essere and a bare job title.
notes: Essere can link you directly to a job title. English needs “a” in this translation.

front: In Sono un dottore, which whole Italian phrase describes who the speaker is?
notes: The speaker and the doctor are one person. Sono links them. Grammarians call this description a subject complement. Compare a direct object in Lavo i piatti.

front: Say “I’m a teacher and I work in a school”. Use fare for the job and lavorare for the place.
answer: Faccio l’insegnante e lavoro in una scuola.
english: I’m a teacher and I work in a school.
pron: FAHT-choh leen-seh-NYAHN-teh eh lah-VOH-roh een OO-nah SKWOH-lah
ipa: /ˈfattʃo linseɲˈɲante e laˈvoro in ˈuna ˈskwɔla/
notes: Laura’s Remember! Join the job and workplace with e. Keep the definite article in l’insegnante.

front: Say “I work as a teacher in a school” using one verb. Give the role and then the place.
answer: Lavoro come insegnante in una scuola.
english: I work as a teacher in a school.
pron: lah-VOH-roh KOH-meh een-seh-NYAHN-teh een OO-nah SKWOH-lah
notes: Laura’s other model uses come for the role and in for the workplace. This repairs the common error lavoro l’insegnante.

front: Food. Complete ___bo with ci or chi and say the word aloud.
notes: Ci gives /tʃi/ here. Start with the ch sound in cheese and pronounce the i.

front: A kilo. Complete ___lo with ci or chi and say the word aloud.
notes: Chi gives /ki/. The silent h keeps the c hard before i.

front: Voice. Complete vo___ with ce or che and say the word aloud.
notes: The c before e sounds like ch in chat. Stress the first syllable.

front: Female friends. Complete ami___ with ce or che and say the plural of amica aloud.
notes: Amica has /k/ before a. Its plural keeps /k/ before e by adding a silent h.

front: A tour. Complete ___ro with gi or ghi and say the word aloud.
notes: Gi gives /dʒi/, starting with j as in jam. Un giro can mean a tour or a lap.

front: A dormouse. Complete ___ro with gi or ghi and say the word aloud.
notes: Ghiro starts like English ghee, with /ɡ/ as in go. Giro starts with /dʒ/ as in jam. The h is silent.

front: An appointment diary. Complete a___nda with ge or ghe and say the word aloud.
notes: Ge starts with /dʒ/, like j in jam. Stress the middle syllable.

front: A line on a page is una riga. Complete its plural ri___ with ge or ghe and say it aloud.
notes: Ghe keeps the /ɡ/ of riga before e. Say the g as in go. The h is silent.

front: A cube. Complete ___ubo with c or ch and say the word aloud.
notes: Before a, o and u, plain c gives /k/. Try the same start in cane (dog), coda (tail) and cubo (cube).

front: A cat. Complete ___atto with g or gh and say the word aloud.
notes: Before a, o and u, plain g gives /ɡ/ as in go. Try gatto (cat), gola (throat) and gufo (owl). Hold the double t in gatto briefly.

front: A shirt. Complete cami___ with ca or cia and say all three syllables.
notes: In camicia, the first i carries the stress. The second i gives the c its /tʃ/ sound before a. Compare farmacia (pharmacy), where the stressed i in far-ma-CI-a forms its own syllable.

front: Yellow. Complete ___llo with ga or gia and say the two syllables.
notes: Gia gives /dʒa/ in giallo. Go straight from the j sound into a, then hold the double l briefly.

front: Use libro. Say “the book”.
notes: Libro is masculine singular and begins with a single l. Its definite article is il.

front: You want an unspecified amount of bread. Use pane and the partitive. Say “some bread”.
notes: Bread is an amount here. In Compro del pane, del means “some”. In il prezzo del pane, the same form means “of the” or “the price of bread”.

front: The children are inside the particular park you mentioned. Use parco. Say “in the park”.
notes: In + il gives nel. Compare in un parco (in a park) with nel parco (in the park).

front: A friend has just come from the park. Use parco. Say “from the park”.
notes: Da + il gives dal for movement from a place. Arrivo dal parco means “I’m coming from the park”. Il cancello del parco is “the gate of the park”.

front: Use zaino. Say “the rucksack”.
notes: Masculine singular zaino begins with z, so use lo. Say dz together. The stressed DZAI rhymes with “eye”.

front: You need an unspecified length of string. Use spago and the partitive. Say “some string”.
notes: Spago is masculine and begins with s + p, so the base article is lo. Di + lo gives dello. Here string is an amount.

front: The keys are inside a particular rucksack. Use zaino. Say “in the rucksack”.
notes: Start with lo zaino. In + lo joins as nello. The double l is held a little longer.

front: You have just walked out of the studio. Use studio. Say “from the studio”.
notes: Studio begins with s + t, so it takes lo. Da + lo gives dallo. Other masculine lo starters include gn in gnomo and ps in psicologo.

front: Use scuola. Say “the school”.
notes: Scuola is feminine singular. The masculine rule for s + consonant does not apply to it.

front: You would like an unspecified amount of pasta. Use pasta and the partitive. Say “some pasta”.
notes: An unspecified quantity of pasta takes the singular partitive. Di + la gives della.

front: The exhibition is inside the particular school you visited. Use scuola. Say “in the school”.
notes: In + la gives nella for this specific building. A scuola is the usual expression for “at school”.

front: You saw smoke coming from the school building. Use scuola. Say “from the school”.
notes: Da + la gives dalla. Here the building is where the smoke is coming from.

front: Use ufficio. Say “the office”.
notes: Ufficio is masculine singular and starts with a vowel. L’ also goes before a feminine singular vowel, as in l’aula (the classroom).

front: You order an unspecified amount of water. Use acqua and the partitive. Say “some water”.
notes: Acqua is feminine singular. Di + l’ gives dell’. Write the next vowel immediately after the apostrophe.

front: The folder is inside the particular office you just described. Use ufficio. Say “in the office”.
notes: In ufficio is a common way to say “at work” or “in the office” generally. Nell’ufficio points to the particular office in this scene.

front: You can hear voices coming from the classroom. Use aula. Say “from the classroom”.
notes: Aula is feminine singular and starts with a vowel. Da + l’ gives dall’. LAO sounds like English “loud” without its final d.

front: Use libri. Say “the books”.
notes: Il libro becomes i libri in the plural. Change the article and noun together.

front: There are some books on the table. Use libri and the partitive. Say just “some books”.
notes: Di + i gives dei. Laura’s Lesson 6 example is Ci sono dei libri, “There are some books”. The number of books is unspecified.

front: The illustrations are in the books you borrowed. Use libri. Say “in the books”.
notes: In + i gives nei. Compare nel libro (in the book) with nei libri (in the books).

front: You copied the quotations from the books. Use libri. Say “from the books”.
notes: Da + i gives dai when the books are the source. Dei libri can mean “some books”, as in Compro dei libri.

front: Use studenti for a mixed group. Say “the students”.
notes: Lo studente becomes gli studenti. Gli is one palatal sound followed by i. The “lyee” guide is approximate.

front: You met a few friends of mixed genders. Use amici and the partitive. Say “some friends”.
notes: L’amico becomes gli amici. Di + gli gives degli. The palatal sound in degli is held a little longer.

front: The lunches are inside the rucksacks. Use zaini. Say “in the rucksacks”.
notes: Lo zaino becomes gli zaini. In + gli gives negli. The Italian plural keeps the z and ends in i.

front: The messages came from the students. Use studenti for a mixed group. Say “from the students”.
notes: Da + gli gives dagli. The students are the senders in Ricevo messaggi dagli studenti (I receive messages from the students).

front: Use amiche for a group of female friends. Say “the friends”.
notes: L’amica becomes le amiche. In the plural the full article le stays before the vowel. The h keeps the c hard.

front: You buy an unspecified number of bananas. Use banane and the partitive. Say “some bananas”.
notes: Una banana is one banana. Di + le gives delle for an unspecified number of bananas.

front: The workshops take place inside several named schools. Use scuole. Say “in the schools”.
notes: In + le gives nelle. Nella scuola is singular. Nelle scuole is plural.

front: You have received replies from the schools. Use scuole. Say “from the schools”.
notes: Da + le gives dalle. Compare dalle scuole (from the schools) with nelle scuole (in the schools).
